new_statements.rule_in_words: Maninka-kan is described as a two-tone (High/Low) language with lexical tonal minimal pairs whose surface pitches are set by utterance-level rules (first High = highest pitch, downdrift, downstep, syntactic tonal dissimilation); the author gives no rule locating a word stress, mentioning stress only to say vowels never reduce under light stress and to contrast Maninka tone with English sentence stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tonal: verbs in final position 'nearly always have low tone'; citation-form HH nouns show dialect-variable final fall (p.12, drill 11 note).
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern lexical tone and utterance-level pitch realisation; citation forms vs sentence forms are distinguished for tone, not stress. Variety is Kankan-centred Maninka-kan with Faranah/Siguiri lexicon, not a Sankaran-specific description (see the note on which variety). Bird (ed.) 1982 p.39 adds, second-hand, a phrase-level 'stress accent' on the last of a run of H-tone words in Bambara dialects and reports Spears' view that Guinean Maninka lowers those highs instead.
new_statements.identity_note: The only Glottolog-listed description of sank1253 proper is Spears 1965 'The structure of Faranah-Maninka' (Faranah is the western anchor of the Sankaran region), which I could not open (ProQuest 302133649; Harvard the Harvard library catalogue online). The open source quoted below, Spears 1973 'Elementary Maninka-kan', is by the same author but is explicitly Kankan-based ('The narratives were recorded by two speakers both of whom were from Kankan. Much of the other material, particularly the lexicon, includes Maninka-kan from other areas such as Faranah and Sigiri', p.vi-vii); Kankan Maninka = Eastern Maninkakan [emk], Glottolog east2426. Its tone chapter is therefore a statement about Maninka-kan generally with Faranah input, not a Sankaran-specific description. Bird (ed.) 1981/82 treats Sankaran as one of the traditional regions around Kankan (section C.4 'Kankan', p.310) and bases that section on Spears 1965, 1973. Glottolog's hh annotation of Davydov 2012 maps his 'Koranko i Sankaran-Koranko' to msc, i.e. that Russian survey may treat Sankaran speech together with Kuranko-like varieties.

sources.note: Ch.1 (p.1-11) segments; ch.2 (p.12ff) 'The nature and function of tone': H vs L tonal contrast, numerous tonal minimal pairs, pitch realisation rules (first H = highest pitch, downdrift, downstep), tonal dissimilation. Only stress mentions: 'Vowels are not reduced to [ə] under light stress' (p.3) and 'The relative simplicity of the consonants and vowels is balanced, however, by a rather complex accentual system' (p.3, meaning the tone system); p.12 contrasts Maninka tone with English sentence stress.
